title: How a chat with Prost inspired Wolff's F1 driver management
excerpt:
Toto Wolff has revealed that a conversation with Alain Prost early in his own Formula 1 career inspired the Mercedes Team Principal in how to deal with fractious relationships between his drivers.

Under Wolff's leadership, Mercedes has secured a plethora of titles and victories, notably with Lewis Hamilton and Nico Rosberg as the Silver Arrows dominated F1 in the mid-2010s.

But this came at a cost, with Wolff having to deal with several flashpoints following on-track collisions in one of the sport's most heated rivalries.

Speaking after last weekend's Singapore Grand Prix, Wolff recalled a conversation he had with four-time World Champion Prost, who had his own legendary rivalry with McLaren team mate Ayrton Senna that resulted in a long-lasting feud even after they raced for separate teams.

"It was very early in my Formula 1 life, I was at Williams, and I remember, as [if] it was yesterday, I was on the grid, and I think he [Prost] was involved in Renault back in the day or something," said Wolff.

"I said to him, I saw it on TV, the whole thing, and how did that escalate between the two of you, almost in a naive way because I didn't understand the dynamics between the drivers, and he said the problem was that you never knew whether you were favoured.

"He said at times I felt that, it was me, it was Alain that was the one that was favoured and then at different stages of the years, it was Ayrton.

"He said that created a dynamic of mistrust in the team and you felt that your direct opponent may be given advantages. Even if it's just emotional at the end the drivers are little traumatised eight-year-olds that were put in a go-kart, they were scared, it was a parent's dream that they were chasing.

"Eventually you end up in Formula 1 and they tell you, now you have to be, you have to play the team game and it's Mercedes or it's McLaren, so it's very difficult."

While not as severe as the Hamilton/Rosberg dynamic, Wolff has had to step in between his current drivers this season, noticeably in Canada when Kimi Antonelli and George Russell went wheel-to-wheel.

But the Austrian believes a transparent and open approach in how the team deals with such issues has made Mercedes stronger, with both Antonelli and Russell obeying team orders this season to help the other driver despite being in a battle for the title.

"You need to feel emotionally protected by the team and I think if you don't do that and you keep it transparent and balanced, that can create moments where the driver just loses confidence and from that learning for me was, okay, I can never do that," he said.

"I need to be transparent, and if one day we decide to play the team game in whatever form, I will say so. I will be saying, these are the rules now, and we'll be very open and transparent.

"And if we have a discussion because the driver disagrees or someone in the team says we should do it differently, then fine, let's have the discussion. So, I would think that this is how we want to behave."

title: Mekies signs long-term contract extension with Red Bull
excerpt:
Laurent Mekies has signed a long-term contract extension to remain as Red Bull's CEO and Team Principal, lasting through the 2031 season.

The French engineer was promoted from Racing Bulls in July 2025 and led the Milton Keynes-based outfit through a challenging start to this year, which saw them drop behind their rivals under the new regulations.

However, their consistent work over the course of 2026 – guided by Mekies – finally paid off as Max Verstappen secured back-to-back victories in Malaysia and Singapore, bringing Red Bull back into contention for regular wins.

With the Dutchman and his team mate Isack Hadjar both receiving contract renewals in recent months, the announcement of Mekies' new deal ensures consistency for the team heading into future seasons.

“I am incredibly proud to continue this journey with Oracle Red Bull Racing, and I would like to thank Chalerm [Yoovidhya], Mark [Mateschitz], and Oliver [Mintzlaff], the entire team, and everyone involved for the trust they have placed in the project,” said Mekies.

“What makes this team special is the way everyone comes together in pursuit of the same goal, and I feel privileged to work alongside such a talented and committed group every day.

“Together, with Pierre Wache’s and Ben Hodgkinson’s teams playing a central role in shaping our future, we have a strong platform for the years ahead, and we genuinely believe this is only the beginning.

“As we look ahead, we will continue to embrace the principles that define us: being free in our thinking, fast in our actions and bold in our decisions.”

Red Bull shareholders Yoovidhya and Mateschitz added: “The strength of Red Bull has always come from its people and from creating an environment where talented individuals can achieve extraordinary things together.

"Laurent has played a crucial role in guiding the team through an important period of transition while maintaining the competitive spirit and the Red Bull principles that define us. This extension reflects our confidence in his leadership and our shared belief in the long-term vision of the team. We are ambitious about what lies ahead and we are committed to building on this momentum together."

Mintzlaff, CEO Corporate Projects and Investments Red Bull, commented: “Laurent has demonstrated outstanding leadership since returning to the Red Bull family. He combines technical expertise, strategic thinking, and a deep understanding of what makes our team successful.

"Just as importantly, he embodies the values and mentality that define the Red Bull way: courage, teamwork, determination, and an unrelenting desire to compete at the highest level. Continuity in leadership is a key ingredient for sustained success, and we are delighted that Laurent will continue to lead the team through the next chapter of our journey.”

title: Freddie Hunt on father James’ legacy 50 years after his title
excerpt:
Freddie Hunt has been reflecting on his father James' title triumph half a century on from the Briton's success and how the iconic driver "glamorised the sport".

It has been 50 years since James Hunt claimed the 1976 Formula 1 World Championship, beating Niki Lauda by just one point in one of the most dramatic title battles in the sport’s history.

The British driver’s triumph came at the season finale in Japan – the exact anniversary falls on the Saturday of the United States GP weekend in Austin – with his rivalry against Lauda and his larger-than-life personality making him one of F1's most memorable and beloved figures.

Speaking on the latest episode of official F1 podcast Beyond The Grid, Hunt’s son Freddie reflected on the anniversary and what made his father such a formidable competitor.

“Fifty years is an awfully long time ago, it’s amazing how the sport has evolved since then,” said Freddie.

“1976 was one of the most incredible seasons in the history of Formula 1. I think that whole era of racing was one of the best.”

Opening up about his father’s greatest strength, Freddie believes it was his ability to adapt, even when his car wasn’t performing as expected.

“I think even when the set-up wasn’t great, he managed to drive around problems,” he explained.

“The first Formula 1 race he won, [the BRDC International Trophy] at Silverstone, the knob on the gearstick broke off, so he did half the race with the spike digging into his hand.

“And then the British Grand Prix in ‘76, because of the hastily-repaired car after the first-lap incident, they didn’t have the set-up right at all. They didn’t have time to.

“He said in the interview afterwards it was understeering an awful lot to begin with, but then it gradually got better. I think he just managed to figure out how to adapt his driving to still go quickly with a wonky car.”

Arguably as famous as his adaptability was Hunt’s fierce rivalry with Lauda, which became immortalised on the silver screen in the 2013 hit film Rush, starring Chris Hemsworth as Hunt and Daniel Brühl as Lauda.

But despite their competitiveness on track, Hunt and Lauda shared a close friendship away from racing, with Freddie recalling an amusing story the Austrian driver once told him.

“They’re opposites, and opposites often attract," Freddie said. "I think they shared the same sense of humour and they were good mates.

“They were testing one day and they had the track. Niki said, ‘James, I’m flying down. If you want a lift in the plane, you’re welcome to, but make sure you’re not late.'

“I think Niki was literally on the runway, revving up the engines, about to take off, and Dad arrives. I think he was a little bit hungover, gets on the plane, puts his music on and has a nap.

50 years since the iconic season that inspired 'Rush'

“Off they go testing, and Dad didn’t come back round. So everyone panics, thinking he’d had a shunt. He’d set some quick lap times, got bored of testing, basically pulled over and had a nap. I don’t think Niki was very impressed!”

Their friendship was particularly evident following Lauda’s near-fatal accident at the Nurburgring in 1976, with Hunt regularly contacting his rival as he recovered in hospital.

“Dad wanted to race against him," Freddie explained. "He wrote to him saying, ‘Get better soon because I need to race against you.'

“He was phoning him every day in hospital and writing to him, cheering him on. ‘Hurry up, get ready, come back quick.'”

Lauda made a remarkable return to racing at the Italian Grand Prix just 42 days after his accident, missing only two Grands Prix. This was despite still recovering from severe burns to his face and head.

Wearing bandages beneath his helmet caused considerable pain given his injuries but the Austrian battled through to finish fourth at Monza. Lauda’s extraordinary comeback kept the championship fight alive, with Hunt eventually securing the title by a single point at the rain-soaked Japanese Grand Prix.

“Dad said he wished they could have shared the championship," Freddie admitted. "They both deserved to win it.”

Beyond his achievements on track, Hunt’s personality helped bring a new level of glitz and glamour to Formula 1, with his influence still felt half a century later.

Reflecting on his father’s legacy, Freddie expressed his pride in how Hunt continues to be remembered.

“He glamorised the sport," Freddie said. "He had a significant impact on F1, I think, and on sport in general. He’s well remembered and it’s lovely. I’m always hearing new stories from people.

“I’m tremendously proud of him. What he did, what he achieved and how he achieved it with humility and integrity. He was much loved.”

title: The 27 tracks Verstappen has won at after Singapore triumph
excerpt:
Max Verstappen triumphed in Singapore with Red Bull at the weekend, to take his maiden Grand Prix victory at the Marina Bay Street Circuit.

The Dutchman won on his 10th attempt under the lights of F1’s original night race to round off an incredible weekend for the four-time World Champion, which also included victory in the Sprint too.

Singapore has long been something of a ‘bogey’ track for Verstappen, despite four previous front row starts and four podiums. His nine starts there without a win was the highest of any current venue on the F1 calendar – but he has finally put that stat to bed with a victory that looked assured from the second he made it to Turn 1 ahead of Charles Leclerc.

Verstappen’s win means he has now tasted victory at 27 different F1 circuits, second only to Lewis Hamilton’s 31. So, where has the Dutchman won, and which are his most successful circuits?

The Red Bull Ring – Austria

Red Bull always seem to go well on home soil and, until Zandvoort joined the calendar, Spielberg was Verstappen’s de facto home race. The orange-clad Dutch fans used to cross the border to Austria in their thousands to cheer him on, and Verstappen more often than not made their journey worthwhile.

He first won there back in 2018, followed that up with another victory in 2019, and then won twice in 2021 when the circuit hosted back-to-back events during the pandemic. His last victory at the Red Bull Ring was a win from pole in 2023, that result coming in the midst of an incredible run of 10 straight victories as he galloped that year to a third straight title.

Wins: 5

Poles: 5

The Autodromo Hermanos Rodríguez - Mexico City

The race in Mexico City is run at high altitude, which often worked well for the Red Bull aero package. As such, Verstappen won back-to-back races in 2017 and 2018 despite his car not being the class of the field across those two seasons.

Verstappen only won two races in 2017 and two in 2018, making it all the more remarkable that victories in Mexico City featured in both seasons.

Three victories in three of his Championship-winning years of 2021, 2022 and 2023 followed, but only one of those was from pole, which makes his results all the more incredible. He was able to share the podium with Mexican team mate Sergio Perez in 2021 and 2022 too, which given the top three park up in the stadium section at the end of the race, must have been quite the atmosphere to experience.

Wins: 5

Poles: 1

Yas Marina Circuit – Abu Dhabi

Yas Marina traditionally hosts the final race of the season, and while some drivers have already taken their foot off the gas and have half a mind on Christmas, Verstappen always turns up with his game face on.

He won in Abu Dhabi four years running between 2020 and 2023, all of those victories coming from pole. His win in 2020 helped springboard his Championship charge in 2021, while his next two wins came at the end of dominant seasons.

He also won from pole there last season, which was not quite enough to clinch the title with Lando Norris’ third place finish enough for the McLaren man to seal the crown. Nonetheless, it is a track Verstappen tends to go well at – not that there are many he doesn’t these days.

Wins: 5

Poles: 5

Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya – Spain

Barcelona was where Verstappen got his first taste of what it felt like to win in F1, in his debut race for Red Bull no less. Having been promoted from Toro Rosso mid-season, he benefitted from the two Mercedes cars colliding at the start and went on to take a famous win at the age of just 18. That made him the youngest-ever winner in F1, a record that still stands today.

He also won in three of his Championship years in 2022, 2023 and 2024, but only once from pole. The other two wins came from second on the grid though, so he is no slouch over one lap in the often scorching hot conditions of Barcelona.

Wins: 4

Poles: 1

Circuit of The Americas - USA

Verstappen has won four out of the last five Grands Prix in Texas, taking victory in 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2025. The first and last of those came from pole, which is not always an advantage in Austin given the long uphill run to Turn 1 that allows for so many different racing lines.

His win in 2023 came from sixth on the grid, the Dutchman made to work hard for the victory after brake issues emerged mid-race. That was his 50th career Grand prix win, a number that has since been dwarfed – his current tally is 73 wins, all with one constructor.

Wins: 4

Poles: 2

Suzuka - Japan

Suzuka is one of those tracks everyone wants to win at and is often cited as the best to drive on the calendar with its sweeping, high-speed corners. Verstappen has won four times in Japan, those victories coming between 2022 and 2025.

His first win was in the wet too, Verstappen giving one of his masterclasses to take not just the victory but also the World Championship crown at one of the most famous venues in motorsport.

The Dutchman’s results have all been built from strong qualifying performances, Verstappen taking all of those victories from pole. He could not make it five from five this season, Red Bull not starting 2026 as strongly as they would have hoped.

Wins: 4

Poles: 4

Autodromo Internazionale Enzo e Dino Ferrari (Imola) - Italy

Verstappen’s record at Imola is truly spectacular. The circuit returned to the calendar in 2020, stepping in as the schedule chopped and changed due to the pandemic. Verstappen might have failed to finish the first race in cold November conditions, but he then won the four subsequent editions.

A win rate of 80% at a track is not to be sniffed at, with two of those victories coming from pole too.

Wins: 4

Poles: 2

Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace (Interlagos) – Brazil

One of Verstappen’s most famous Brazil drives was not for the win, the Dutchman scything his way through the field in treacherous, wet conditions back in 2016 to bag a podium. But he has taken victory at Interlagos three times, from pole in 2019 and 2023, and then from P17 on the grid in 2024.

That last win was another masterclass from the Dutchman in wet conditions, as he survived red flags and plenty of chaos to not just climb back through the field, but win by nearly 20 seconds in an imperious display of car mastery.

Wins: 3

Poles: 2

Lusail International Circuit – Qatar

One of the newer editions to the calendar, Qatar has hosted four Grands Prix so far, in 2021, 2023, 2024 and 2025. Verstappen has won three of them for a 75% success rate, buoyed by often having the best car towards the end of the season, such are Red Bull’s development strengths.

He has only taken pole once, back in 2023 when he beat George Russell over one lap by nearly half a second. Last year, the Dutchman won from third on the grid with Red Bull nailing their strategy calls to help Verstappen beat the McLaren pair, which at the time ensured the Championship fight would go to the last race of the season.

Wins: 3

Poles: 1

Circuit Gilles-Villeneuve – Canada

Montreal is another circuit that can throw up chaotic races, not to mention the Wall of Champions that has caught many a famous driver out over the years.

Two of Verstappen’s three wins have come from pole in 2022 and 2023, the other in 2024 coming from second on the grid. He also has three other podiums here, and yes, he has hit the famous wall back in 2024, fortunately doing so in practice.

Wins: 3

Poles: 2

Autodromo Nazionale Monza - Italy

The Temple of Speed rewards cars that have good low-drag set-ups, something Red Bull have not always necessarily had as a strength. But Verstappen still has three victories at a track where speed is everything, winning in 2022 and 2023, before grabbing victory from pole in 2025.

This was not his best track in his early career, the Dutchman failing to finish on the podium in his first seven outings here, with reliability woes also not aiding his cause. But a win from seventh on the grid in 2022 changed that, Verstappen beating Leclerc as he finally got to stand on the top step of one of the most impressive podiums in the sport.

Wins: 3

Poles: 2

Circuit de Spa-Francorchamps - Belgium

Spa is another home race for Verstappen, and not just because so many Dutch fans can make their way to the Ardennes Forest relatively easily. His mother is Belgian, although Verstappen races under the Dutch flag like his father.

Like Suzuka, Spa is one of those historic tracks everyone wants to win at, with Verstappen doing so for three consecutive years from 2021. His 2022 win was from 14th on the grid, the Dutchman’s car the class of the field as he made light work of recovering from grid penalties in one of his title-winning years.

Wins: 3

Poles: 1

Circuit Zandvoort – The Netherlands

Zandvoort joined the calendar in 2021, with Verstappen winning the first three editions of his home race. All of those wins were from pole too, the Dutch fans not minding his dominance one bit as they enjoyed watching their man do what he does best.

Verstappen followed those wins up with two second-place finishes, but sadly his final Dutch Grand Prix saw him crash out early after dipping a wheel onto the slippery white lines following some earlier rain.

Wins: 3

Poles: 3

Jeddah Corniche Circuit – Saudi Arabia

Another relative newcomer on the calendar, Jeddah is a fast, exhilarating street track that has caught out more than one driver since its first race in 2021. But thus far, Verstappen’s record there is fairly eye-catching, with two wins and three second-place finishes from the five editions so far.

While he has two poles at the track as well, his best result is arguably his P2 in 2023, achieved from 15th on the grid after a driveshaft failure cost him in Qualifying. The issue returned late on in the race, leaving the Dutchman no chance to try and challenge Perez ahead for the win.

Wins: 2

Poles: 2

Sepang International Circuit – Malaysia

Verstappen was the last driver to win in Malaysia back in 2017, the circuit then dropping off the calendar. But it reappeared in 2026 as host of the Bahrain Grand Prix, and the Dutchman picked up where he left off.

He won from third on the grid in 2017 for what was then just his second-ever F1 victory, but in 2026 the four-time World Champion put an at times difficult season to bed with his first win of the year, from pole no less.

Wins: 2

Poles: 1

Las Vegas Strip Circuit – USA

Verstappen won the inaugural Las Vegas Grand Prix in 2023, having to work hard for the win after picking up a time penalty in a slightly chaotic race that saw several Safety Car periods, the Dutchman overtaking Perez and Charles Leclerc late on to take the victory.

He won again last year as part of his late charge to the title – which ultimately saw him come up just short in Abu Dhabi.

Wins: 2

Poles: 0

Baku City Circuit – Azerbaijan

Baku has not always been a happy hunting ground for Verstappen, who has had a few brushes with the walls over the years here. He crashed out when leading in 2021 thanks to a tyre issue, while 2018 will long be remembered for a collision between Verstappen and his team mate at the time, Daniel Ricciardo.

But Verstappen does have two wins at the street track, winning in 2022 before taking victory from pole in 2025. He came agonisingly close to a third victory this season, just unable to out-drag Russell’s Mercedes across the line.

Wins: 2

Poles: 1

Hungaroring – Hungary

The Hungaroring near Budapest is reminiscent of a karting track and is another one the drivers love, but it lends itself to a very specific car set-up, and is somewhere Red Bull have not always excelled. Verstappen recorded back-to-back victories in 2022 and 2023, but has not won there since while his only pole was back in 2019.

His win in 2022 is the highlight, Red Bull nailing their strategy as Verstappen recovered from P10 on the grid, pulling off multiple overtakes and even surviving a late spin to beat Lewis Hamilton and Russell.

Wins: 2

Poles: 1

Miami International Autodrome – USA

Miami joined the calendar in 2022, with Verstappen taking the inaugural win. He followed that up with victory in 2023 too, but since then things have not gone entirely to plan in the Sunshine State.

Poles in 2024 and 2025 did not yield victory, while this season Verstappen trailed home in fifth-place in a car that Red Bull were still fighting to understand.

Wins: 2

Poles: 2

Circuit de Monaco - Monaco

Verstappen’s first Monaco victory came in 2021 from second on the grid – but with pole-sitter Leclerc unable to take the start, the Dutchman was de facto P1. He won from pole in 2023 as well, but this street track has not always been his forte.

He has only started from the front row three times at a circuit where grid slots are everything, while this season, anti-stall cost him off the line before he was forced into retirement with more mechanical woes.

Wins: 2

Poles: 1

Bahrain International Circuit - Bahrain

Verstappen’s two wins in Bahrain came in 2023 and 2024, when his Red Bull was the class of the field. Both years Bahrain was hosting the opening race too, meaning Verstappen’s season got off to the best possible start.

He also has three poles at the desert track, along with two other podiums. And the record books will state he has won three Bahrain Grands Prix, having taken victory in Malaysia this season which was hosting on behalf of Bahrain.

Wins: 2

Poles: 3

Silverstone – Great Britain

Given how often Silverstone throws up some questionable weather, it might be something of a surprise that Verstappen has not won more than twice in Northamptonshire. His first victory was the 70th Anniversary Grand Prix in 2020, and he won again in 2023.

That second victory came from pole, while the two other times he started P1 did not go so well – an infamous collision with Hamilton ending his race early in 2021, while he trailed home fifth in 2025 despite the race being held in those wet-dry conditions he normally favours.

Wins: 2

Poles: 3

Circuit Paul Ricard – France

France last hosted a Grand Prix in 2022, with Verstappen winning that edition from pole position. He has raced at Paul Ricard four times, winning in 2021 as well, while 2018 yielded a podium and 2019 saw him come home in fourth-place.

Wins: 2

Poles: 1

Albert Park – Australia

Melbourne has not always been kind to Verstappen, the Dutchman failing to finish three times at Albert Park with mechanical gremlins. But he has won there just the once, back in 2023 when he took victory from pole.

He also started on pole in 2024, but brake issues did for his race that season.

Wins: 1

Poles: 2

Shanghai International Circuit – China

Verstappen only has two podiums in China from eight attempts, one of those a victory back in 2024 from pole. His record might have been improved had Shanghai hosted a race during some of Red Bull’s dominant years, the circuit not featuring on the calendar for four years from 2020.

Wins: 1

Poles: 1

Hockenheim – Germany

Verstappen won the last German Grand Prix to be held back in 2019, a humdinger of a race that saw the Dutchman pit five times in rainy conditions, yo-yoing his way from the back to the front as Red Bull excelled with their strategy calls – helped no end by Verstappen’s input from the cockpit.

On a day where many drivers were left looking a little foolish in tricky conditions, Verstappen again underlined why he was rated so highly, something that has not changed in the subsequent years.

Wins: 1

Poles: 0

Marina Bay Street Circuit - Singapore

Finally, the one that got away so many times but not in 2026. Singapore throws up some of the hottest, most humid conditions of the season, which has not always favoured Red Bull. The team won three times with Sebastian Vettel, while Perez also took a win under the lights at Marina Bay.

But finally in 2026, Verstappen had the car, the speed in Qualifying, made no mistakes and was able to tick off a new track, having now stood on the top step of the rostrum at 27 different venues.

Wins: 1

Poles: 1

Could Verstappen add to his tally in 2027?

There are three venues on the calendar for next season Verstappen has not yet won at – Portimao in Portugal, the Madring in Spain and Istanbul Park in Turkey.

Verstappen has raced at all three, with second-place in Turkey his best result from two efforts, while he bagged two podiums in two attempts at Portimao.

The Madring joined the calendar for the first time this season, with the Dutchman finishing second to Kimi Antonelli.

title: 'We owe him one' – Mekies on Hadjar's Singapore issues
excerpt:
For Isack Hadjar, the Singapore Grand Prix weekend proved to be one to forget after a nightmare series of technical issues impacted almost every track session.

Even on race day things didn’t go perfectly to plan, but he was at least able to put in a storming charge from the pit lane to finish 10th.

After the race Red Bull Team Principal Laurent Mekies was quick to apologise for the problems that denied Hadjar the chance to show what he could do, noting that “we owe him one”.

Hadjar arrived at the final race of the triple header on the back of his superb drive to third in Azerbaijan, and frustration in Malaysia after a late power unit glitch saw him lose another potential P3 as he slipped back to fifth.

In Singapore things started to go wrong in Friday’s Sprint Qualifying as he again had PU issues, and had to settle for P9.

“What seemed like a good start of the day turned into really very poor performance,” he said. “I never got to have a good lap really, I'm just fighting with the car, had engine issues on the last run. Just struggling. I don't know, it's just weird.”

Saturday proved to be even worse when he suffered a PU failure on the third lap of the Sprint. A great effort from the RBR crew saw him switch to previously used elements for Qualifying.

However, from the start of the session he suffered a gearbox issue – the result of a perfect storm of events going wrong – and having lost fourth gear he was not able to do a flying lap. To add insult to injury, after he parked up the car was doused with extinguishant.

“Today was a disaster,” he rued. “I could have stayed back in Paris, and it would have been the same…”

The team was left with a lot of work to do, and it was decided to break parc ferme, add a new power unit to the pool, and start from the pit lane.

At the start he lost out initially to fellow pit lane starter Fernando Alonso as once again PU issues struck, but thereafter he found the pace to move up the field. He eventually made it to P10, finishing just 6s behind George Russell, who had started from 19th on the grid.

“It was good for everything that's happened,” Hadjar said after the flag. “Definitely good pace, but I don't know what to say. It's just surprising we could make that race entertaining, considering it's very difficult to overtake around that track. I'm quite happy about that. But I would have liked to make use of that pace to fight for a win.

“I just sent it, but at some point I thought this is a train, I'm never going to finish in the top 10. And then on that soft tyre, I knew I had good pace to unlock, but I didn't think I would be that fast. So that was nice.”

To his credit, he was keen to praise his crew for their hard work: “It was challenging for my mechanics. They suffered quite a lot for just one point. So it's definitely their weekend, and they deserve better. So we try again.”

Mekies stressed that the team had let Hadjar down with the reliability issues.

“We had a pretty horrific weekend on his side of the garage,” said the Frenchman. “We basically didn't give him any chance to do any competitive laps before the main race on Sunday.

“We had a number of different mechanical issues – some on the PU, some on the gearbox, some other glitches. So it was really like a nightmare weekend.

“In that context, the crew – not only Isack's crew, but it also was fully involving Max [Verstappen]'s crew who helped – the other side of the garage was under the car changing massive components all weekend long up to this morning in parc ferme before the race start, which is probably not what you want on the last of three in a triple header in hot and humid weather.

“So huge, massive congrats to the to the crew for what they've done. I've never seen such an incredible turnaround, and to then deliver a faultless race car on Sunday. Nonetheless, we have lost the chance to see Isack's speed here. So we owe him one.”

Mekies was impressed with what Hadjar was able to achieve despite the problems: “In the race, starting last and spending 90% of the race in traffic, he still showed very, very strong pace, which only confirmed that he would probably have been up there on the sharp end of the classification.

“So it's on us. But he certainly has shown that he had the speed with a few laps he done on Sunday.”

Verstappen’s domination of the Singapore weekend with two poles and two wins indicated just how competitive the RB22 is at the moment, and Hadjar is keen to bounce back with a clean weekend at the US GP.

“Now since Malaysia, I'm just desperate to have a car that's working a bit better on my side to fight for a win,” he said. “Because at the moment, it's not possible to fight. So now we need to reset, understand what happened since Sunday in Malaysia, and make sure to come back in Austin and fight for podiums.”

title: The upgrades behind Red Bull’s breakthrough in Singapore
excerpt:
For the first 14 races of the season, Max Verstappen found the Red Bull RB22 a very difficult car. But a breakthrough was made with a major upgrade in Baku for Round 15, one which subsequently allowed Verstappen to win the next two successive races, at Sepang and Singapore.

He spoke about progress after taking his first-ever Singapore victory last Sunday. “The last few races have been really positive for us,” Verstappen said.

“Our car has taken a really nice step forward. It's just been more driveable and more predictable. That's what I wanted and needed from the car to find that last step to fight up front. And I hope that we can carry that momentum forward…

title: Inside the making of Netflix’s Schumacher ’94
excerpt:
Among the footage that stayed with Christin Freitag after making Schumacher ’94 – The Birth of a Legend was an interview with a spectator at Hockenheim. Asked by a television reporter whether the noise was too much, the man in glasses replied: “No, not at all. Wonderful, wonderful.”

The footage captures the growing enthusiasm for Schumacher in Germany during the season in which he claimed his first Formula 1 World Championship, something Freitag was particularly interested in exploring through the archives.

Released on Netflix on October 2, the documentary follows the then-25-year-old Benetton driver from his opening victory in Brazil to the title decider in Adelaide. It features interviews with his wife Corinna, former Benetton Team Principal Flavio Briatore, Bernie Ecclestone, David Coulthard and his manager Willi Weber, among others.

“That’s what we were trying to accomplish – you don’t look from the outside or look back, but you really transport yourself into the time, into this extreme season of Formula 1, and be right there with him,” Freitag tells F1.com.

Searching through 1,300 hours of footage

The major races would inevitably feature, such as the tragic events at Imola and the championship decider in Adelaide. But Freitag and editor Bobby Good also went looking for less familiar moments.

“When you’re new to a subject, you don’t know what you don’t know, so there’s always the possibility of finding interesting stuff,” she explains.

“We had a structure, but we scanned everything. I think we had 1,300 hours of footage from the races and my editor, Bobby Good, was relentless in searching through everything.”

She adds: “All the races tend to look the same after some time. You have the suits, the helmets, the tracks. But you spot straight away when something interesting or real is happening in people’s faces, or with Michael.”

Freitag also planned when interviewees would recount events in the present tense, placing their memories alongside the footage.

“I was trying to build a very narrative structure that really pulls you into the story," she says. "I knew I needed a lot of archive footage for it to be immersive, so I thought maybe 60 or 70 per cent should be archive footage.

“I essentially wrote a script. I knew which scene came when, what protagonists I needed for each scene, and what led to what. It’s basically film-making construction.”

Ralf Schumacher on his brother and ‘idol’ Michael

Finding the sound of the 1990s

The soundtrack combines original scoring with music from the decade, including Pulp’s Common People and Paula Abdul’s Rush Rush, a song that holds particular significance for Michael and Corinna.

“It’s important to have songs that transport you right into the time, but the editing is so precise to the music that it was necessary to score a lot of things,” Freitag explains.

“With the score, it was also a process of finding the right tone. You want to feel like you’re in the ’90s, but you don’t want everything to be the same. It has to be modernised in a way that transports you back, but makes it better in a way.

“It’s a mixture of finding songs where they can live and have space, and then there are a lot of scenes that rely on music, but more on the rhythm, so you have to score them.”

The decision to include Common People, released in 1995, towards the start of the documentary was less deliberate than some of the other musical choices.

“I just loved the song," Freitag laughs. "We had a collection of ’90s songs, and a lot of ’90s songs really hurt my ears! It was a gut feeling, more or less. That it also fit was a bonus.”

Revisiting Imola

The 1994 San Marino Grand Prix remains one of the darkest weekends in Formula 1 history. After Rubens Barrichello suffered a serious crash in Friday qualifying, the sport was shaken by the deaths of Roland Ratzenberger during Saturday qualifying and three-time champion Ayrton Senna during Sunday's race.

“I knew it had been portrayed many times, and I watched closely how it had been portrayed,” Freitag explains. “Whenever you go into the story, you already know what’s going to happen. There’s this heaviness hanging over the whole weekend.

“I wanted to make something that takes you through the weekend as everybody back then lived through it. You come into it totally unprepared, quite light-hearted in a way. The mood is good. You’re going into a race weekend in Italy. It’s going to be a very exciting race.

“And then it happens out of nowhere. Then something happens again, and again.”

Even after shortening the Imola footage, difficult editing choices remained.

“You’re in the middle of it and can’t believe it’s happening, that it’s not stopping, and that it’s getting worse and worse,” she says. “I wanted to recreate that experience of being in the weekend, reliving this trauma.”

Senna also features later in the documentary, with the link between the great Brazilian and the German extending far beyond that tragic weekend. In 2000, Schumacher became emotional at Monza when asked about what it felt like equalling Senna’s total of 41 Grand Prix victories.

“I wanted [Senna] to still be there because I feel he’s always there with Michael, always at the back of his mind,” Freitag explains. “He carried it with him all those years, so I knew it was very central to him.”

Discovering a different Schumacher

For Freitag, throughout her experiences working on the documentary, she got to discover far more about the seven-time champion that she ever thought she would.

“I was surprised by the person I found, because growing up I knew him much later, in the 2000s, when he was already the legend," she says. "I was surprised that he comes across as quite sensitive. You feel the way he’s protecting this sensitivity, and you can also see where he puts on a show, or where this diverges and he becomes somebody else.”

In one archived English-language interview, Schumacher discusses his fears after Imola, giving Freitag access to his own account of the season.

“When I was interviewing all the other people, I was searching for this specific character trait, because I had always thought he was so fearless, so ruthless,” she says.

“But in the archive, especially in this interview, I see a totally different Michael. I was searching for this guy. Is that the real one? Does he have a protective shield, or is that just one moment in time? That formed my picture of him, my feelings towards him, a lot. I centred the film around it.”

Willi Weber, who managed Schumacher during his rise through F1, was one contributor whose recollections supported what Freitag had found.

“A lot of the protagonists solidified this picture of Michael as someone without fear, someone very straightforward – except Willi, his manager, who was very close to him,” she says.

“He solidified what I’d seen in the archive. He said Michael was totally different after Imola, that it really changed him.”

Corinna and the people who knew him

Corinna Betsch, Michael’s girlfriend in 1994, is another central figure. The couple married the following year, and the documentary includes her memories of their early relationship and entering the F1 world together.

“I also like that they came into this circus as a couple, both very fresh, and discovered it together,” Freitag says. “I like the way she wasn’t impressed by it at all. She found it rather boring, and then developed an interest in it.”

Freitag met Corinna through the production company to discuss the documentary before filming their interview.

“She was so light-hearted and fun," she adds. "That jumped out at me. She had such a lightness about her, and I wanted to bring that across in the film because I hadn’t seen it in previous interviews.”

However, the documentary also reveals aspects of Schumacher's experiences that Corinna was unaware of at the time. In an archived interview, Schumacher spoke about struggling to sleep following Senna's death at Imola, admitting that he had begun to fear for his own life, even away from the circuit.

“Corinna is aware of the interview, but she wasn’t aware that he actually had those fears or feelings in that moment,” Freitag says. “Both are true. It’s interesting, and it expands the depth of the character.”

Other contributors offer different perspectives on the 1994 season. Briatore was Schumacher’s Team Principal at Benetton, while Coulthard made his F1 debut with Williams at the Spanish Grand Prix following Senna’s death. Former F1 boss Bernie Ecclestone also appears, as do German television personalities Kai Ebel and Heiko Wasser.

“I did a lot of research about many characters and spoke to a lot of people. I narrowed it down from a storytelling perspective: who’s crucial to which moment?” Freitag explains.

“But also, in the pre-interviews, who would open up the most? Who would really give me some closeness to the main character?

"It was also important to balance these stars with people behind the scenes who you haven’t heard of. I like that mixture.”

Capturing Schumimania

The documentary also records the role of television in Schumimania. Broadcaster RTL was helping F1 reach a wider German audience, while the Hockenheim archive showed the fans gathering near the circuit.

“The scene at Hockenheim is a bit of a love letter to a German soul that has disappeared,” Freitag says. “I remember it from growing up. It raises memories, and that world isn’t there any more. It’s like a love letter to a past time.

“I knew I wanted this scene, and then I found this great footage of the camping area. That was amazing. I think there were three or four hours of interviews with the fans… It was a gift.”

Freitag also considered why spectators identified so strongly with a driver who did not always appear at ease with his growing celebrity.

“He doesn’t seem super outgoing or charismatic in the sense of entertaining a crowd. So why do Germans love him so much?” she says. “That’s what Willi always said: ‘He’s one of us.’”

At the final Grand Prix in Adelaide, Schumacher and Damon Hill arrived separated by just one point. Their collision ended both races, leaving Schumacher to claim his first World Championship.

“For sure at the end [of the film], when he became World Champion for the first time,” Freitag says when asked when Schumacher became the figure remembered today.

“It’s really the starting point of his legend. The whole film is before the legend. It’s only at the end that the legend is born. It’s the road to becoming this legend.”

title: Inside Rwanda’s plan for the African Grand Prix
excerpt:
“It will be remembered as one of the most significant days in the history of Formula 1,” said President and CEO Stefano Domenicali, upon the announcement that the championship will hold an African Grand Prix from the early 2030s.

Returning to Africa has been an ambition for F1 for a protracted period but finding the right location, with the right long-term viability, has been a crucial factor. Now, Rwanda provides that platform.

Only two countries in Africa have so far held a World Championship Formula 1 Grand Prix. Morocco’s Ain-Daib road course made a one-off appearance in 1958, while South Africa was visited on 23 occasions, most prominently at Kyalami, but it held its final Grand Prix in 1993.

Rwanda has been up-and-coming within the sporting landscape; Kigali hosted the FIA Awards in 2024 while in 2025 the country held the week-long UCI Cycling World Championships, the first nation in Africa to do so. It will now add a round of the Formula 1 World Championship to its events roster.

It is part of a process not just to develop Rwanda as a tourist, sports and entertainment destination, but to become a focal point for the rest of the continent too, in part explaining the African Grand Prix moniker.

“For decades, African athletes have been a pillar of the global sports economy, adding significant commercial value to top leagues, with the continent receiving almost nothing in return,” said Rwanda’s President, Paul Kagame, at the announcement. “Partnerships like the one we are building help break this cycle.”

Kagame accepted that “we are a small country” but steadfastly believes in using sport as a mechanism to further develop the nation, and the wider continent.

“Formula 1 is part of the big picture of what Rwanda has to build, there are many things that Rwanda has undertaken to do and we have made progress as a country and as a people,” he said.

“But also for Formula 1, we are not looking at just Rwanda alone, we are looking at Rwanda in the context of a continent, and we have ambitions to bring in other African brothers and sisters to participate.”

The announcement of a 10-year contract enables Rwandan officials not just to develop a circuit for the sake of hosting a Grand Prix, but to accelerate the presence of the sport in the continent. Based on previous new race locations, data shows that Formula 1 events typically generate in excess of £100 million of annual economic impact for the host nation.

F1 returns to Africa with 10-year deal to race in Rwanda

“We want to make it bigger than just Rwanda,” explained Jean-Guy Afrika, CEO of the Rwanda Development Board. “We want to make it the moment when the sport came back to Africa and then never left.

“We felt that calling it ‘Kigali Grand Prix’ or ‘Rwanda Grand Prix’ would have felt slightly exclusive. You know, it's much easier if you call it an African Grand Prix, to approach partners in this wide effort.

“We foresee a future where we look back at this moment and we see a critical juncture from where multiple races eventually end up happening in Africa.

“I think it will be very thrilling for these young generation of Africans that love the sports and that have been looking for opportunities to experience the sport not on television but in person.

“You've already seen that the interest [in Africa] was very high. We weren't the only ones bidding, and we expect that after the first race, there probably would be many more races.”

Rwanda will join the calendar in the early 2030s but it first requires a circuit – and that is the task facing Carsten Tilke of renowned designers Tilke Engineering, and ex-F1 racer Alex Wurz of Wurz Designs.

Fortunately for the pair, Rwanda’s location within the Great Rift Valley means it is known as the ‘land of a thousand hills,’ and there are grand plans for the venue, positioned in Bugesera, close to where Kigali’s new international airport is due to open in early 2028.

Wurz has been involved in the project for several years and explained: “One of the first decisions was what sort of circuits and what location should it be?

“There were discussions about a street circuit, relocating elsewhere, maybe occupying the old airport, and multiple locations came up. When we learned about the development in Bugesera, and then we actually saw it, and you see the hillsides and the lakes, I said, ‘guys, there's only one location this circuit should be, because it doesn't need us to design it, because the nature designed already the perfect topography.

Everything we know about F1's all-new race in Rwanda

“’It's two hills with the lake below, that means we can drive up and down the beautiful landscape and we want to live a picture-perfect African Rwanda landscape.’”

The 6km anti-clockwise circuit is planned to feature 17 corners and has been designed for a wide range of motorsport disciplines. The full track layout has not yet been released but Wurz has completed “thousands” of laps in the simulator, there will be 197 metres of elevation change across a lap, as well as cambered turns and banking.

“It was always important for us that it's amazing to drive, challenging to drive, but on the other hand, also creating great races,” Tilke said. “So we needed to create overtaking points, we needed to make sure different strategies are possible on that track and so on, so that we have a nice Qualifying but also a nice race.

“The other thing very important for us was [that] the focus was always the spectator. Spectators must be close to the track, must feel the track, must be part of it. It really is a roller coaster track.”

That extends to the facility itself, which will feature paddock buildings typical of Rwandan architecture, incorporating the village ethos and classic red dirt look, while the multi-purpose facility is also intended to be utilised for concerts and other major events.

The investment also includes a karting facility – in order to focus on long-term grassroots support – as well as a driving experience centre and off-road courses.

Kigali is located around 1,500 metres above sea level, which will make it one of the highest circuits on the calendar, with Mexico City at 2,200 metres. That has an impact on the performance of machinery, and Wurz says that is being factored into simulations.

“That means we have less pressure in the air, that means also less grip from the aerodynamics,” he explained. “So we can counter that with some of the cambers.

“[In simulations] we are playing heavily with slight camber changes at times when you have degradation on the front or the rear, we consider what tyre temperatures are coming into corners, so that the defending driver actually is at disadvantage for the next long straight.

“There's a lot of science as well as knowledge from the years of driving and designing tracks going in.

“I can tell you it's going to be a drivers’ track. If you believe me a little bit, it's going to be one classic of a track immediately. I hope that this circuit is the cherry on the cake on everyone's list.”

title: Who impressed our Power Rankings judges in Singapore?
excerpt:
Max Verstappen was in a class of his own in Singapore last weekend, as he finally claimed victory at the Marina Bay Street Circuit. But who else impressed our Power Rankings judges? Check out the latest scores and overall leaderboard below...

How it works

Our five-judge panel assess each driver after every Grand Prix and score them out of 10 according to their performance across the weekend – taking machinery out of the equation

Our experts’ scores are then averaged out to produce a race score – with those scores then tallied up across the season on our overall Power Rankings Leaderboard (at the bottom of the page)

Verstappen had one thing on his mind last weekend: winning around the streets of Singapore at the 10th attempt. Making the most of Red Bull’s recent updates, which yielded a first 2026 win at Sepang the weekend before, the Dutchman was unstoppable through Sprint Qualifying, the Sprint, main Qualifying and the Grand Prix itself. Our judges deemed it to be a perfect display.

Liam Lawson is fighting for his F1 future once more as F2 championship contender Nikola Tsolov knocks on the door of a promotion at Racing Bulls. The New Zealander has been doing all he can to keep hold of a seat, though, with his SQ3/Q3 and double points performance at Marina Bay the latest in a long list of impressive displays.

Charles Leclerc emerged as Verstappen’s closest challenger as the Singapore Grand Prix weekend developed, qualifying second to the four-time World Champion and pushing him hard over the early laps of the race. While he did not quite have enough pace to challenge for the win, second marked a strong result for the Monegasque and Ferrari.

Nico Hulkenberg has just missed out on points several times this season, but the German was twice rewarded for his efforts at the Marina Bay Street Circuit. While Audi could not reach SQ3/Q3, Hulkenberg made the most of the drama ahead to bag a couple of points in the Sprint, and then maturely raced his way to eighth in the Grand Prix – keeping Mercedes’ George Russell at bay in the closing stages.

Kimi Antonelli had a battle on his hands throughout the Singapore weekend, as the Italian pressed on with Mercedes’ recent updates while team mate Russell reverted to an older package. After a tricky Sprint Qualifying, Antonelli appeared to make progress in understanding the W17’s new ways during the Sprint, before taking a much-improved P4 in main Qualifying and then turning that into a podium on race day – one that puts him on the brink of securing the 2026 title.

Ollie Bearman led the Haas charge again under the Marina Bay lights, getting the better of outgoing team mate Esteban Ocon in every session. The highlight was a run to P6 – and some important points – during the Sprint, where he pounced on McLaren’s intra-team clash. While he did not have enough speed to score more in the Grand Prix, he impressed with some fine midfield moves at unconventional overtaking spots.

Lewis Hamilton had looked set to join team mate Leclerc on the podium in Singapore, even after starting on what proved to be the less favourable medium tyres. However, while Leclerc pitted for fresh rubber under a mid-race Virtual Safety Car, Hamilton stayed out on the softs he had switched to early in the race – a provisional P3 turning into P6. In the hours after the chequered flag, Hamilton apologised for taking the strategy into his own hands, admitting that much more was possible given the raw pace he had displayed.

Oscar Piastri’s weekend started well with a solid run to P4 in Sprint Qualifying, ahead of team mate and reigning World Champion Lando Norris. Drama followed in the Sprint, though, when Norris tagged the Australian into a spin – and into the wall – on the final lap of the race. Norris held the upper hand again across Qualifying and the Grand Prix, with Piastri’s efforts in the main event hampered by a slow puncture.

While Williams’ difficult 2026 season continued in Singapore, Carlos Sainz comfortably led the intra-team battle over Alex Albon across the weekend. He turned a pit lane start into P12 in the Sprint, made it into Q2 in main Qualifying, and then battled his way to 14th in the Grand Prix, appearing to get everything he possibly could out of the troubled FW48 machine.

Pierre Gasly once again caught the eye over one lap last weekend as he dragged his Alpine into SQ3 and Q3, giving himself and the team a chance of scoring some crucial points in their championship battle against Racing Bulls. He came agonisingly close to doing so in both the Sprint (crossing the line ninth) and Grand Prix (placing 11th).

Missing out

Just missing out on the Singapore Power Rankings list are Norris, following the collision with Piastri that he has since apologised for, and Isack Hadjar, who climbed from the pit lane to points on race day after a weekend hampered by technical problems.

title: McLaren answer vital question after 'doubts' and 'very weird' concern
excerpt:
McLaren boss Andrea Stella has said the Singapore Grand Prix helped prove that the team had not made the MCL40 slower with its Baku-specification upgrades, having initially had "doubts" on that front.

Andrea Stella has revealed that McLaren feared its Baku upgrade package had made the MCL40 slower, with the team only able to put those doubts to rest after the Singapore Grand Prix.

The Woking-based squad introduced a significant bodywork update at Baku, featuring reworked sidepods and cooling, aimed at boosting straight-line speed around the Azerbaijan circuit's long back straight.

But Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri struggled for pace there and at the following round in Bahrain, leaving the team unable to isolate whether the upgrade itself was to blame.

Matters were not helped by what Stella described as "very weird" data from the Sepang circuit, where unusually rough asphalt disrupted McLaren's usual correlation between trackside readings and its simulation tools.

Speaking to media, including RacingNews365, Stella explained the uncertainty that built up over the two rounds.

"If we take Baku and Malaysia in isolation, we were not very competitive," said the McLaren team principal.

"We had doubts about the package we introduced in Baku; we never expected it to be a big step from a lap-time point of view.

"But because we upgraded two cars at a single time, we had no comparison. We thought, 'Have we made the car slower?'

"At least we were in condition to clarify that that's not the case, which is an important question that we were able to answer in Singapore, going back to a track that is just a little bit more normal than Malaysia, where the track roughness just made the data look very weird. But we understand that it had to do with the track roughness."

[Article continues below]

Baku and Sepang slump

McLaren has endured a sharp downturn compared with last season, when Norris and Piastri regularly fought for wins — and the former won the F1 drivers' title to go with a second successive constructors' crown.

This year the team has had to settle for third in the constructors' standings, 239 points adrift of runaway leaders Mercedes and in danger from Red Bull behind with the gap now just seven points.

That is despite Norris being the class of the field in Hungary, Zandvoort and Madrid, where he won twice and finished third.

Since then McLaren has slipped badly, with Norris ninth at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia and fourth in Singapore, while Piastri has not finished higher than fifth across the last four rounds.

Stella pointed to specific technical factors behind the Azerbaijan Grand Prix and Sepang slump.

However, he was pleased that the final leg of the triple-header offered some much-needed clarity.

"And Baku, in which we think that the power unit optimisation played a significant role in terms of lap time," the Italian added.

"We know that this is not only power unit optimisation; there are a few more things on the chassis side that, in the long straights, penalise McLaren in the current configuration, like the [gear] ratios.

"So we had doubts for a couple of races, but we welcome the fact that we were able to clarify that there's nothing wrong going on..."

title: Audi extends long-running partnership into Formula 1 era
excerpt:
Audi has marked a new chapter in its long-running relationship with Öhlins by confirming the suspension specialist as its official supplier.

The Swedish company, which became part of the Brembo Group in January 2025, has been working with Audi on a joint development programme covering engineering, testing and damper performance since before the team's grand prix debut back in March.

That groundwork has now been formalised into an official partnership, coinciding with Audi's first campaign in Formula 1.

The deal is not Öhlins' first involvement with the Ingolstadt manufacturer. Between 1999 and 2016, Audi Sport competed at the 24 Hours of Le Mans using Öhlins dampers across several generations of its sports prototypes, a period that yielded 13 overall victories at the French endurance classic.

Öhlins also supplied dampers for Audi's DTM programme in the 2000s, including for the Audi A4 DTM that was introduced in 2004.

Discussing the new agreement, Öhlins Group Engineering Director Urban Herslöf said the partnership represented a significant point in the company's motorsport history.

"We are proud to partner with Audi Revolut F1 Team in its debut season," said Herslöf.

"For Öhlins, this is a defining moment for our legacy in motorsport, and a powerful platform for us to extend our collaboration with Audi and help shape a new era of automotive performance."

title: Max Verstappen explains Kelly Piquet feelings towards racing outside F1
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has explained how partner Kelly Piquet feels about his decision to keep racing GT cars on weekends away from Formula 1.

The Red Bull driver will head to Portimão for the GT World Challenge Europe Endurance Cup finale in the gap between the current triple-header and the Americas triple-header, sharing a Mercedes-AMG GT3 with Chris Lulham and Ben Barnicoat.

It leaves Verstappen with just a single free weekend across the final 11 rounds of the F1 season, amounting to seven consecutive weekends of racing.

The four-time F1 drivers' champion already runs his own outfit, Verstappen Racing, which competes in GT World Challenge Europe, DTM and Nürburgring endurance events through partnerships with teams including 2 Seas Motorsport, Emil Frey Racing and Winward Racing.

Verstappen himself has raced at the Nordschleife, including a class win at an NLS round last year and a stint leading this year's Nürburgring 24 Hours before a mechanical failure ended his race.

Asked how Piquet views his busy extracurricular racing schedule, Verstappen told media, including RacingNews365: "I think it helps that she comes from a family that races a lot. So I think she can understand a lot better [than most].

"Honestly, I always try to also combine stuff. So even if, let's say, you would be racing, maybe you can combine it with going around with the family a little bit, even at a race weekend like that."

[Article continues below]

Verstappen reveals Piquet 'doesn't mind' his extra racing

Piquet, the daughter of three-time F1 drivers' champion Nelson Piquet and sister of Nelson Piquet Jr., has a racing pedigree of her own.

She shares a daughter with Verstappen and has a son from a previous relationship with former F1 driver Daniil Kvyat.

The Dutchman added that compromise is key to balancing the demands of family life with his packed schedule.

"So we're trying to see what we can do there, but at the same time, she knows that I need to feel good and just be happy also, right, for both sides," Verstappen said.

"So we just try to always find compromises from my side, from her side, and try to spend as much time yeah together within.

"But she doesn't mind it. I think she likes racing; it's not that she's against it, so that helps."

title: Toto Wolff pokes fun at Kimi Antonelli with 'little cushion' quip
excerpt:
Toto Wolff could not resist the urge to make a joke at Kimi Antonelli's expense after the Italian flirted with a track limits penalty at the Singapore Grand Prix.

Antonelli came precariously close to picking up a five-second time penalty during the 62-lap race at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, reaching his final warning.

It has been a persistent issue for the 20-year-old in what will become his first F1 drivers' championship-winning season, and race engineer Peter Bonnington was heard stressing the importance of not overly pushing the limits over team radio.

It ultimately would not have mattered, with Antonelli taking the chequered flag in third, 16 seconds ahead of Lando Norris in fourth.

Antonelli's penchant for trick limits strikes is perhaps his last significant rough edge for Mercedes to smooth over, and Wolff was quick to address it after the race.

The Mercedes team principal used humour to defuse his underlying point, suggesting that Antonelli needed a pillow on his seat to help see the white lines of the circuit edge.

"Kimi, well driven. Well done," Wolff said over team radio before getting in the playful dig.

"Maybe we need to have a little cushion under you; have you sit higher with the track limits, but it was very good."

Sky Sports F1's Martin Brundle also enjoyed the comment, adding that Wolff "never wastes an opportunity" on broadcast.

title: Christian Horner explains why huge potential Red Bull partnership collapsed
excerpt:
Red Bull spoke to several potential partners ahead of the 2026 F1 regulations, including one giant German manufacturer.

Christian Horner has explained why Red Bull's proposed partnership with Porsche for the 2026 power unit regulations never materialised, detailing how the collapse paved the way for Ford's arrival instead.

Red Bull spent part of 2022 in discussions with Porsche over a tie-up built around the new engine rules, which did away with the costly MGU-H and introduced a near 50-50 split between combustion and electrical power.

The Volkswagen-owned manufacturer saw the new regulations as its route into Formula 1, and initial conversations progressed as far as Red Bull founder Dietrich Mateschitz exploring the idea with Porsche and Horner visiting its base in Weissach.

But the deal ultimately fell through, with Porsche's demand for a 50 percent stake in Red Bull Technology proving a sticking point. Horner, speaking to Autosport, said there was hesitation within the group over whether Red Bull could build a competitive engine on its own, before Porsche emerged as an option.

"I think there were still some nerves within the group within Austria that, really, could we produce a competitive engine?" Horner said.

"And then Porsche suddenly came as a possibility, and I think in Dietrich's mind, by this stage, he wasn't in great shape. But he saw the benefit of the Porsche brand, an amazing brand. A Red Bull-Porsche was really premium.

"They make engines, we don't, and so we explored that. And I went to Weissach and saw some of their facilities and recognised that we were miles ahead in terms of what we were doing in preparation for Formula 1 compared with where they were, and it felt like there were going to be a lot of compromises bringing these two entities together, with perhaps challenges in the direction of a 50-50 partnership.

"And so that deal didn't go through in the end. But we needed a partner because it was a big burden. I was very conscious, in turning the Porsche deal down, that the whole engine [programme] was sitting on Red Bull's hands."

Why Ford left Christian Horner immediately impressed

With Red Bull Powertrains shouldering the cost of both retaining Honda's technical support and developing its own 2026 engine, alongside running teams, the outfit's former team principal turned his attention to Detroit.

There, Ford was weighing a return to the sport, with Horner having been left immediately impressed by the American manufacturer's enthusiasm.

The agreement was formally announced in February 2023, with Ford contributing expertise on electrification, battery architecture and control software while Red Bull Powertrains retained managerial independence over the project.

Horner added: "Not only were they (Red Bull) paying for Honda to stay in Formula 1, they were paying to build their own engine [for 2026], and of course, Red Bull also has two grand prix teams, and so Ford Motor Company were looking around Formula 1 at the time, and I went to Detroit and had a meeting with Bill Ford and Jim Farley, and straight away you could see there was an enthusiasm for them to come.

"And having been involved in the team in its previous iteration, Bill Ford said to me, 'We're going to let you guys... You're the specialists. The learnings that we had from our last experiences, we don't want to over-involve ourselves in your business. How can we help you? How can we support you?'

"And so that partnership got going in time for the '23 season."

title: South African minister fires punchy response after Rwanda handed major F1 contract
excerpt:
South Africa's Minister of Sports, Arts and Culture, Gayton McKenzie, has delivered a punchy response after Formula 1 confirmed Rwanda as the host of a new African Grand Prix on a 10-year contract, insisting the East African nation's success does not mean South Africa has lost out.

F1 announced this week that it had signed a decade-long agreement to race in Rwanda from the early 2030s, with the event set to be staged at the newly planned RISE Motordrome in Bugesera, roughly 40 kilometres south of the capital Kigali.

The purpose-built venue, designed by Tilke Engineers & Architects alongside Alexander Wurz's WurzDesign, is being developed to meet FIA Grade 1 standards and sits next to Rwanda's new international airport.

South Africa has long chased its own return to the F1 calendar, with a previous push to revive the Kyalami circuit collapsing ahead of the 2023 season after promoters failed to meet Formula One Management's financial guarantees.

Speaking during a media briefing, as reported by Independent Online (IOL), McKenzie congratulated Rwanda directly before pushing back on suggestions his country had been overlooked.

"I want to congratulate Rwanda for being awarded a spot on the F1 calendar in a year in the 2030s," McKenzie said. "Now, we in South Africa, we're very happy that Rwanda has been awarded a spot, and I want to talk directly and congratulate the president of Rwanda, the Rwandanese [people], and the minister, who is a very good friend of mine. I would like to congratulate her.

"So I've seen many comments of people saying, 'Oh, South Africa was beaten, South Africa was beaten.' So, I want to address that issue. This is not a raffle. I'm going to repeat that. This is not a raffle.

"Rwanda has applied years before I even thought I would be a minister of sport, agriculture. Rwanda has done the work. We came on board. I was appointed, and I followed what F1 wanted us to do. Now, applying for a spot on the F1 calendar, we are not in competition."

South Africa pushing for F1 return before inaugural Rwanda event

McKenzie went on to insist that South Africa still intends to bid for a grand prix of its own, targeting a slot before the end of the decade with fresh commercial backing lined up.

"Now they say Rwanda has beaten us," added McKenzie. "No, Rwanda has not beaten us. We as South Africans are looking still at 2028, 2029. Rwanda has done what they needed to do.

"We are South African. We have spoken to the most important people, which are the sponsors.

"We've got MTN. We've got Betway. We've got Discovery, we've got Canal+, and the big one I can't announce because it's going to be at our function of one of the biggest banks, is partnering with us, which I can't mention now because we're going to have another function where we're going to announce it."

title: Exclusive: Red Bull name Max Verstappen F1 trait 'no other driver' is capable of
excerpt:
Red Bull technical director Pierre Waché has pinpointed the one F1 trait he believes Max Verstappen has which "no other driver" is capable of.

Verstappen is a central pillar in the rebuild underway at Milton Keynes under Laurent Mekies - and has recently guided the team to its first two grand prix victories with its own in-house Red Bull Powertrains engine.

The Dutchman, a winner of 73 grands prix and four world titles, is renowned for being demanding of his team for a car which suits his driving style - which relies upon a razor-sharp front-end on initial corner turn-in.

During the opening laps of a grand prix weekend in the first practice, it is often Verstappen who initially climbs to the head of the times with an early opening salvo whilst he and the team work to dial the car in - with Waché describing how this feedback the 29-year-old gives the team is unlike anything he has experienced.

"I think the main benefit that he has is the feeling he has of the car," Waché told RacingNews365 in an exclusive interview.

"I will not call him an engineer, because he is not, but he is giving the engineer something that no other driver I saw can, in terms of feedback and identifying exactly what is needed to be quicker.

"It is insane the capacity he has to feel the car, what is missing when he is driving it, and afterwards to be able to translate that into a world we can understand.

"After the first lap [of practice], he knows exactly where the car is, where the limit is, and he is the best driver I think the sport has ever had, and what makes him even better is that he is able to say: 'Yeah, I am missing that, I miss that, I miss that.'

"When we are winning, he is a dream. When we are losing, he is a nightmare; I'm joking, but as an engineer, we love him because he gives us performance. He gives us very good feedback, and he is a team player. That is why we like him."

[Article continues below.]

Verstappen respect all around

Waché also touched upon the respect Verstappen and the engineering team hold, and how Verstappen is open to new ideas.

"Maybe his engineer [Gianpiero Lambiase], but I don't want to know; I don't want to give him my phone number and be called in the middle of the night," Waché quipped, when asked if Verstappen had ever called him in the middle of the night with an idea.

"No, no, but he respects what we are doing, and he respects the team. He respects the job of everybody, and he just gives his feeling of what is important to him, but he respects our expertise, what he thinks, what we think, and he is quite open-minded.

"He is quite easy to work with, and he is not arrogant in the way he works."

"It makes me happy when we are winning. I am here for that. If I am not winning, I will not be here."

title: Kimi Antonelli sends clear message as first F1 title opportunity looms
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli stands on the precipice of winning his first F1 drivers' championship, but the Italian is adamant that the mindset that got him to this position cannot change now.

Kimi Antonelli has insisted he will not get carried away by the prospect of sealing the F1 drivers' championship at next weekend's United States Grand Prix, despite holding a commanding 102-point lead over Mercedes team-mate George Russell.

The 20-year-old Italian could be crowned champion at Circuit of the Americas if he extends his advantage to 125 points or more, based on the assumption that five rounds remain after Austin.

That margin required will shrink to just 100 points if Formula 1 opts to scrap the Qatar and Abu Dhabi double-header in favour of a single replacement race at Imola, a scenario still under consideration amid ongoing security concerns in the Middle East.

No final decision has yet been made, with clarity by mid-October expected given freight and logistical deadlines.

Asked how much he would allow himself to dream about clinching the championship in Austin, Antonelli struck a measured tone.

"For sure, but at the same time, I know it's very close; I know it's there, but I just need to make sure that I keep doing the best I can," he said to media, including RacingNews365.

"The mindset is always the same: to go out there and win and perform the best way I can."

[Article continues below]

Antonelli planning to 'reset' before COTA

Antonelli's third place in Singapore, where Russell could only manage ninth, has further cemented his position at the top of the standings on 340 points, with the Briton on 238.

Even a difficult weekend extended his lead, and the Italian now looks set to wrap up the title at COTA or, at the latest, in Mexico City.

The Mercedes driver was candid about his display in Singapore, where he finished on the podium despite admitting it was far from his sharpest weekend of the campaign.

"I think [in Singapore] I haven't particularly driven that well," Antonelli added. "I felt like I could have done a better job, but I feel confident that a week to reset [will help], and I'm really looking forward to being back in Austin.

"But at the end of the day, if I don't do my job well, then the result won't come. So in order to achieve what I want, I need to perform, as simple as that."

title: Lewis Hamilton proposes major F1 shake-up after 'epic' realisation
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has proposed the idea that more F1 grands prix should be run at night after his "epic" realisation about the Bahrain GP.

On the original 2026 calendar, six races - Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, Las Vegas, Qatar, and Abu Dhabi were set to be run at night, with there remaining the possibility that only Singapore and Las Vegas go ahead owing to the Middle Eastern races being cancelled due to the Iran War.

This sextet of races marks one-quarter of the 24-race calendar being run at night, with Bahrain originally serving as a day race when it joined the calendar in 2004, with the 2005 race being measured as the hottest grand prix in history, with temperatures peaking at 42.8 degrees Celsius

For 2014, the race shifted to a night race, and has been a staple of the calendar since.

But F1's first night race was the 2008 Singapore Grand Prix, with Hamilton recalling over the recent Marina Bay weekend conversations held with Bahraini officials over its race time - and how more races could make the switch in future.

"I love the night races. I remember when this one was being brought on, and we did the test on the simulator back in the day when I was at McLaren," Hamilton recalled of the first Singapore GP to media, including RacingNews365.

"It did obviously an amazing job with the lighting, and then we've had that at other places. I remember speaking with [Crown Prince] Salman, and we were testing and running in Bahrain in the middle of the hottest day ever, and the tyres and whole cars were melting.

"I said: 'This place will look epic at night', and then years later, they ended up doing a night race there.

"So I think in some places it works really well, particularly really extreme hot places, where if you're in the middle of the day, like in Qatar, it's probably going to be miserable for the fans, but also for everyone in the paddock.

"So some of the night races, I think, are really cool. We were just in Madrid, and it's beautiful during the day.

"I was like: 'This could also be cool at night, and many of the tracks could be.'

"So who knows? Maybe having the option to switch between that over time would be a cool development for tracks."
