title: McLaren identify Oscar Piastri 'signature' key to ongoing F1 struggles
excerpt:
McLaren boss Andrea Stella believes Oscar Piastri's "signature" driving style has not translated well into the 2026 F1 car - as he has had to "abandon" some traits.

Piastri claimed seven grand prix wins in 2025 and led the world championship for 15 races in total before the late-season struggles meant he finished third behind team-mate Lando Norris and Max Verstappen.

The Australian has scored just two grand prix podiums in the all-new 2026 F1 cars, where the machines generate their downforce in a different manner to the ground-effect machines, with the rear of the car also moving around a lot more as opposed to the planted, stable rear of 2025.

Piastri has 138 points to Norris's 201, with it now being 14 grands prix since his last podium finish, a third place in Miami.

As he continues to work through the issues, his team principal believes that it has simply taken the Melbourne-native longer to learn to adapt his "fast and clean" driving style to the 2026-era cars.

"The car needs quite a lot of effort to deliver lap time, and it requires a level of intensity in the driving input, which is much superior to last year," Stella told media, including RacingNews365.

"This is something that took some time for the drivers to get comfortable. Well, comfortable is wrong, but to get to understand, and it's also one of the reasons why Oscar almost looks like he lost some of the competitiveness compared to Lando.

"We were discussing what is happening with Oscar, and I've always said that that was a technical matter. Oscar just needed to understand how to force the car to do some things and sort of abandon the fact that driving fast will not necessarily mean driving clean.

"Instead, probably the signature of Oscar, when we have seen him fast in the past, was that he was clean. It was really good data to see.

"It was very repeatable, and it was fast. With this car, all these things together don't seem to happen very often. So it's a lot of work for the drivers."

[Article continues below]

Stella on making McLaren easier to drive

Stella has confirmed that McLaren will be bringing a fresh upgrade package towards the end of the season - but does not believe it will make the 2026 machine easier to drive.

"I don't expect that what's coming to the car will improve this characteristic," he added.

"I think we need something more fundamental than simply adding some downforce to the car, like it's happening in the coming races, without fundamentally changing some further aspect, which we are addressing longer term, I would say with the MCL41 for 2027."

title: Max Verstappen taking on Valentino Rossi raises intruging questions
excerpt:
Max Verstappen goes up against Valentino Rossi this weekend at Portimão. The MotoGP legend's former BMW team-mate Kelvin van der Linde (centre in headline image) is in the unique position of knowing what the four-time F1 drivers' champion can expect.

14 October 7:10PM

Max Verstappen will share a track with Valentino Rossi for the first time in a competitive setting this weekend, with the pair set to go wheel-to-wheel at the GT World Challenge Endurance finale in Portimão.

Verstappen lines up in a Mercedes AMG GT3 EVO, while Rossi will be behind the wheel of a BMW M4 GT3 EVO. The four-time F1 drivers' champion has already made clear he would rather not run into the MotoGP legend out on circuit. But is there really anything for Verstappen to worry about?

Few people are better placed to answer that than Kelvin van der Linde. The South African BMW factory driver spent a lengthy spell as Rossi's team-mate and has shared a car with the Italian on several occasions, giving him a unique insight into how the nine-time MotoGP champion has adapted to four wheels.

Speaking to RacingNews365 earlier this year, Van der Linde gave a frank assessment of where Rossi stands as a GT racer.

"It's a tricky question," he says. "I think that success in MotoGP came because he just had an incredible talent for two wheels.

"He was in the prime of his career back then. He was the perfect age at that time. Now, stepping into GT cars, he's in a different age category."

"I think even the very best drivers struggle to still be at their peak at 46. If I look at my own future, around my 45th [birthday], I'd be very happy if I was still competitive. But that is kind of the age where it gets difficult, isn't it?"

Van der Linde stressed that the transition has been anything but straightforward for Rossi, who made the switch to four wheels in 2022 with Team WRT before joining BMW in 2023.

The Italian, he explained, had to put in far more groundwork than a driver who had come up through the GT ranks.

"It meant that whole dynamic was harder for him. He had to put in a lot more work to be fast in a GT car. After all, he came from a different background."

Rossi's relentless work ethic

Van der Linde highlighted Rossi's work ethic and meticulous attention to detail as a combination that, even now — racing on four wheels instead of two — sets The Doctor apart from his rivals.

"What I did notice is that he is an incredibly hard worker, and I think that's something that characterises all the real top guys: that attention to detail," he said.

"He wants to know everything about the car. He wants to know anything that could give him even the smallest advantage. And when he's paired with a factory driver like me, he asks endless questions until he gets the answer he's looking for."

However, he also pointed out that due to the Italian's age and late coming to racing cars, he lacks an edge of speeds compared to those around him.

"In terms of pure talent, I think he's also very talented in a car," Van Der Linde stated. "But like I said, time and age have kind of passed him by a bit since he started in GT racing, he was already over 40 by then.

"So I think he was very competitive, and still is, but you have to see everything in relative terms. I say that with the utmost respect for Valentino.

"He's a great endurance driver, and he'll keep having success as an endurance driver in future too. But those last two, three tenths... it's a bit too late for him for that."

© XPBimages

What Verstappen and Rossi have in common

It is not just about outright pace, either. Van der Linde admitted he has picked up plenty from Rossi off the track too, much of it mental, and something he also recognises in Verstappen.

"Mental things, more than anything else. I think the way he deals with his fans is still remarkable," he explains.

"I mean, that guy is an icon and just has so much patience for fans and for signing stuff and so on. That's a level of dedication that I really admire, because as GT drivers we don't have that kind of fanbase.

"But sometimes, when you're having a bad day, that's not easy either, right? Then you've got a fan who expects you to be happy and smiling.

"That's nowhere near my level, nor is it Max's or Valentino's, and that's actually why I admire them both. They're quite similar in their patience, and in how they deal with their fans, it's very admirable."

title: Red Bull announce long-term extension for 'outstanding' F1 boss
excerpt:
Red Bull boss Laurent Mekies has signed a new-long term contract with the team, until the end of the 2031 F1 season.

The news was announced by Mark Mateschitz, the son of late founder Dietrich, during a team debrief at Milton Keynes following Red Bull's victories in the last two grands prix in Bahrain and Singapore.

Mekies, who replaced Christian Horner in the role in July 2025, helped to reignite Max Verstappen's faltering title defence that season, as he embarked on a strong run at the end of the season, only narrowly missing out on a record-equalling fifth successive title by two points.

Under Mekies, the team has also completed its journey of becoming a power unit manufacturer in its own right, with Verstappen taking the landmark first win in Sepang.

The renewal of the Frenchman's contract until the end of the 2031 season is the latest for Red Bull in recent weeks, with Verstappen and Isack Hadjar also agreeing new contracts to stay, as well as other team members as the post-Horner rebuild continues.

"I am incredibly proud to continue this journey with Red Bull Racing, and I would like to thank Chalerm [Yoovidhya] Mark, and Oliver [Mintzlaff] (below), the entire team, and everyone involved for the trust they have placed in the project.

"What makes this team special is the way everyone comes together in pursuit of the same goal, and I feel privileged to work alongside such a talented and committed group every day."

Prior to joining Red Bull, Mekies was the team principal and CEO of Racing Bulls, having also enjoyed previous spells in senior positions at the FIA and Ferrari, and started his career at Arrows in 2001, before moving to Minardi in 2002, which, over time, would be known as Toro Rosso, AlphaTauri, and currently Racing Bulls.

[Article continues below]

Red Bull senior figures praise Mekies

The shareholding of Red Bull is split between the Voovidhya family, headed by Chalerm, and Mateschitz, and in a joint statement, the pair spoke of the "crucial role" Mekies had played in rebuilding the team.

"The strength of Red Bull has always come from its people and from creating an environment where talented individuals can achieve extraordinary things together," it read.

"Laurent has played a crucial role in guiding the team through an important period of transition while maintaining the competitive spirit and the Red Bull principles that define us.

"This extension reflects our confidence in his leadership and our shared belief in the long-term vision of the team. We are ambitious about what lies ahead and we are committed to building on this momentum together."

Oliver Mintzlaff, the CEO of Corporate Projects and Investments at Red Bull GmbH, and therefore responsible for both the company's F1 teams, added that Mekies had "demonstrated outstanding leadership since returning to the Red Bull family.

"He combines technical expertise, strategic thinking, and a deep understanding of what makes our team successful.

"Just as importantly, he embodies the values and mentality that define the Red Bull way: courage, teamwork, determination, and an unrelenting desire to compete at the highest level.

"Continuity in leadership is a key ingredient for sustained success, and we are delighted that Laurent will continue to lead the team through the next chapter of our journey."

title: Two-time F1 champion kicks off world’s longest sabbatical - On This Day
excerpt:
Mika Hakkinen finished fourth in his final grand prix, in Japan, on this day, October 14, 25 years ago. The two-time F1 drivers' champion had decided to take a sabbatical in 2002, but he would never return.

14 October 6:20PM

Mika Hakkinen walked away from F1 after the 2001 Japanese Grand Prix and never came back, yet twenty-five years on, the Finn has still never formally announced his retirement.

What began as a one-year sabbatical from McLaren, with Kimi Raikkonen drafted in as his replacement for 2002, simply became permanent. No press conference, no farewell tour. Hakkinen just didn't return.

The 2001 finale at Suzuka was won by Michael Schumacher, his ninth victory of a season he had wrapped up with races to spare.

Juan Pablo Montoya finished second for Williams. Third place belonged to David Coulthard, but only because his McLaren team-mate handed it to him five laps from the end.

Hakkinen, running fourth, moved aside on the main straight to let Coulthard through, a gesture with history behind it.

"I'm happy that David finished on the podium. I must admit that by letting him past I wanted to give him something back for the occasions in the past when he has helped me," Hakkinen said, recalling favours at Jerez in 1997 and Melbourne in 1998 when Coulthard had done the same for him.

Coulthard, for his part, kept his reaction brief in the FIA press conference. "It's nice to finish the season, as Michael said, on the podium," he said.

Driver

Mika Häkkinen

Finnish

A title fight that wore him down

By the time Hakkinen climbed out of his McLaren that day, the decision to step away had already been made. It traced back to the opening race of the season in Melbourne, where a high-speed suspension failure sent him into the barriers and dragged up memories of the near-fatal crash he suffered at Adelaide in 1995.

"When they were doing that, it all suddenly reminded me of my Adelaide accident. I was in the same country, and again a technical problem had caused me to crash," Hakkinen said at the time.

"When something like that happens to you again, you start to think in a very negative way. [...] I sat down and thought to myself, 'You've won two championships; one should never be too greedy'."

The birth of his son Hugo in December 2000 had already begun shifting his priorities away from the single-minded obsession that two world titles, in 1998 and 1999, had demanded.

Hakkinen approached Ron Dennis at Monaco in May 2001 intending to retire outright, only for the McLaren boss to talk him into calling it a sabbatical instead, keeping the door open for a return in 2003.

"At the Monaco Grand Prix in 2001 I informed Ron that I wanted to stop, but he wanted to make sure that I made the right decision and gave me the opportunity to take a sabbatical," Hakkinen said. "Once I had spoken with Ron a huge weight came off my shoulders."

The Finn who never came back

McLaren turned to Raikkonen, then just 21 and with barely a season of car racing experience at Sauber behind him. Dennis backed the gamble on raw speed over CV, and Hakkinen himself endorsed the choice, pointing to the composure the young Finn had already shown.

The sabbatical was never reversed. Reportedly, during his year away, Hakkinen realised he felt relief rather than restlessness, and that the motivation to return simply never came back.

A flirtation with a comeback resurfaced in late 2006, when he tested for McLaren and held talks with Williams, but a Barcelona test that November exposed how much the demands of testing and reliability had moved on, and the idea was shelved for good.

Schumacher, the man who denied him further titles, later named Hakkinen as the rival he respected above all others. "The most respected guy in all those years was Mika Hakkinen. Great fights but a stable private relationship," he said.

Hakkinen has never stood in front of a camera and said the word retirement. He simply stopped turning up, and Formula 1 moved on without him.
